chapter: Big bands, small groups and studio work
title: Learning the Carmen Jones pit score

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Carmen with a whole colored cast and it's going to be a hit, Cozy, believe me, I wouldn't tell you to leave CBS here to go over here with this show if I didn't think it was going to be a hit." Well, Russell Bennett was conducting the pit orchestra.

Oh yes. Well, I said yeah, John, I'd like that, you know. He says Cozy, your name will be in the Playbill and you'll do a stellar performance up on stage. Now he never said anything about the pit right then. Then later on, he says Cozy, they need two drummers in the pit. Now could you be one of those drummers? And I had never, that's a semi-opera, Carmen, I'd never did that before, but at the time I was studying up at Julliard, and I was used to following a conductor from working in those workhouse bands, workshop bands there at Julliard, I was used to following a conductor, so I said yeah, because I only had to play in the pit was castinet, triangle, bass drum, snare drum and wood block. Hand cymbql.
And you were playing traps on stage?

I was playing a full set on stage. So I told John, I said "John, do you know what would be good," John Hammond. "If I could get that score." I'm frightened to death 'cause I never did this before, and as you know the opera Carmen, the first thing that this when that conductor comes down is those hand cymbals (HUMMING) .... and I said

oh my goodness, here I am going to build my whole career, I says if I miss that, the rest of the band is going to say where the hell did you get that drummer from, you know. But I did it and I knew how to follow the conductor. Of course the other drummer in the pit played the tympani and vibes. So, I went to rehearsal frightened to death, now, I never did this before, in the pit, had a big band, had about 18 or 20 fiddles from the New York Philharmonic, bassoons, bass horns and everything, all sitting in the pit and in the pit here I am way over here and the bass is way over there across the street, so that's hard to hear you know. But anyway they brought the music out, I looked at the music, the music didn't look hard, you know, the whole score. It was numbered one, two, and cut from two to eight you know how to draw that line and cut, So I sit there and we got through with the intro and everything was cool and so they'd sit down and rest for a while and then of course with a show, they're always going to cut this out and cut this out and cut this out, so at the time, goodness, they were just cutting segments of the music out and it gave me chance to peep a little while and look and see what was happening you know, and by doing that, man, it made it so much easier, because a lot of times I'd play about eight bars and the whole orchestra would stop and say all right we're going to cut from number 18 we're going to the second 16th note in bar 30. So you do that, and everybody take their time

and we rehearsed about two weeks, then we took the show on to Philadelphia and New Haven and Boston. Altogether about three weeks out on the road before we came into New York. Well by then I knew the score backwards. Everybody did. You know, everybody. You knew the score backwards. When you hit New York, you could play with your eyes closed, because I was so used to playing shows with Cab, Benny Carter, Willy Bryant, whereas the average Broadway show is two hours long, isn't it, you would say?
